title: A slide rule multiplies numbers by adding two lengths

cover.alt: Close-up of the finely engraved scales on the slide of a Keuffel & Esser slide rule.

body: On a slide rule's C and D scales, each number sits at a distance from 1 that is proportional to its **logarithm**, and the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms: log(x × y) = log x + log y. So sliding one scale along the other adds two lengths, and the number you read off is the product. William Oughtred combined two of Edmund Gunter's logarithmic rules into a recognisable slide rule around 1622, shortly after John Napier published the idea of logarithms. It stayed the everyday calculator of science and engineering, good to about three significant figures, until cheap pocket calculators arrived in the mid-1970s.

slides.alt: Animation of an ivory and bamboo slide rule with a glass cursor. The numbers on its scales crowd together as they grow, every doubling takes the same step, and sliding the C scale works out 2 × 3 = 6 and 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 by adding two lengths.
slides.music: “Study And Relax” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Work out 2 × 3: drag the slide so its 1 sits over 2 on the D scale, then move the cursor to 3 on the slide.
slides.takeaway: The cursor reads 6 on D. Distances on the scales are logarithms, so putting two lengths end to end adds log 2 and log 3, which is log 6.

slides.alt: Buzz Aldrin in a spacesuit inside the dark, cramped Gemini capsule, with a pipe in his mouth and a slide rule floating near him.
slides.caption: Buzz Aldrin on Gemini 12 in 1966, with a slide rule floating beside him. His own Pickett slide rule later flew with him to the Moon on Apollo 11.

slides.question: A slide rule shows 6 for 2 × 3, and also for 20 × 30. How do you tell which answer is which?
options: You track the decimal point yourself
Use the back of the rule
slides.explanation: The rule only gives the digits. Users worked out the size of the answer separately, in their heads or with scientific notation, to place the decimal point.

slides.question: The HP-35 of 1972 was the first handheld scientific calculator. What did it cost, in US dollars of the day?
slides.explanation: $395: fine for some engineers, too much for most students. By 1976 the TI-30 sold for less than $25, and the slide rule's days were numbered.

slides.heading: Still in some cockpits
slides.text: One slide rule is still in daily use around the world: the E6-B flight computer, a circular slide rule for aircraft navigation. Many sailors also keep a slide rule as a backup for navigation in case the electrics fail.
